kicker: THE FILES · FEATURE · FILED UNDER: LOST THE STORY · 1769–1821 · STATUS: STILL TALKING
label: Lost the story
title: Not a Loser. Not Short. Not Alone.
dek: He conquered Europe believing power meant armies, borders and crowns. A poor island outsider trained as a soldier, he never learned to beat the other kind: the bankers, insurers, admiralties and trading companies that ran the sea lanes above any government. Whose man was Napoleon, really?
summary: How France’s 1799 Brumaire coup was planned by government insiders, staffed with Napoleon as a hired general, and paid off for Paris bankers.

blocks.text: I1 · THE PUPPET. Everyone wanted a hand on him.
France’s own government insiders planned the takeover. The money men waited behind the curtain. The famous general was the last piece they added.
The Story You Were Told
A brilliant young general sails home from Egypt. France is a mess. He marches into Paris, grabs power in two days, and the grateful nation hands him the keys.

Now look at the facts. Napoleon had just walked away from his own army in Egypt. He had no political party and no money of his own. He landed in the south of France on October 9, 1799. Thirty-one days later he ran the country.
Nobody does that alone. Somebody opened the door.
The Job Posting
In 1799 France was run by five men called the Directors. One of them, a sharp ex-priest named Emmanuel Sieyès, decided to overthrow the government he was part of.
Sieyès had the plan. What he lacked was a general with soldiers who would follow orders. He is said to have told friends he was “looking for a sword.”

items: His first pick, General Joubert, was killed in battle in August 1799.
His second pick, General Moreau, said no.
His third pick stepped off a boat in October.

blocks.text: According to one famous story, when Moreau heard Napoleon had landed, he told Sieyès: “There’s your man. He’ll do your coup better than I would.”
Napoleon did not start this plot. He applied for it.
The Enemy’s Newspapers
So what made Napoleon leave Egypt in the first place? The British handed him the news.

In early August 1799, a British naval commander named Sir Sidney Smith passed the French a bundle of English and German newspapers. They carried news up to June 10, and it was all bad for France. Its armies were losing in Italy and Germany. Three weeks later, Napoleon slipped out of Egypt at night. He left the newspapers for the general he abandoned, with a note: “You will see that we have lost Italy.”

Did Britain lure him home on purpose? The record says no. British accounts say ships were posted to catch him, but they were off getting food and water when he sailed. Admiral Nelson had ordered that not one Frenchman leave Egypt. Smith most likely sent the papers to make the French army lose heart.
If so, it backfired. A British officer’s bundle of newspapers helped send home the man Britain would fight for the next sixteen years.
The Crew
Every job needs a crew. This one was stacked with the most powerful insiders in France.

items: The Architect: Sieyès. A sitting Director. He wrote the plan and the new constitution to go with it.
The Fixer: Talleyrand. The former foreign minister, famous for switching sides and getting rich doing it. He brought Napoleon and Sieyès together and handled the deals.
The Cop Who Looked Away: Fouché. The police minister. The man whose job was to stop plots against the government let this one run.

The Inside Man: Lucien Bonaparte. Napoleon’s 24-year-old brother. Two weeks after Napoleon landed, Lucien was elected president of the lower house of the legislature. That timing saved the whole operation.
The Yes Man: Roger Ducos. A second Director who went along.
The Writers: Roederer, Cabanis and Boulay. Speechwriters and legal minds who handled the paperwork and the public story.

blocks.text: The Cop Who Looked Away
Joseph Fouché became police minister in July 1799, four months before the coup. His job was to know about every plot in Paris.

A historian who later read Fouché’s daily police reports from those months found “not one word” about Napoleon or the plan to overthrow the government. Paris was buzzing with rumors, and the police reports said nothing.

Fouché’s own memoir goes further. He says the war minister tried to warn the two Directors who weren’t in on the plot. He sent them a police agent who knew the whole scheme. The agent escaped out a window and ran to Fouché. Fouché says he then worked to erase the warning from the Directors’ minds, and he told Napoleon about it.

Fouché also had his own cash. He found more than 700,000 francs in the police till. He rented out the right to run the gambling houses of Paris for 80,000 francs a month. After the coup, the price jumped to 180,000. In the three months before the coup he spent more than 230,000 francs, and no one has shown what that money bought.

One memoir by a former secret agent claims Fouché handed over 900,000 francs of police money on day two, “once the scuffle was over,” to pay the coup’s bills. No document backs that up. What the record does show is a police minister with a full cash box and empty reports.
The Script
The plan ran like a heist movie.

Step 1: Invent a threat. On the morning of November 9 (18 Brumaire on France’s revolutionary calendar), the upper house was called to an early meeting. Members likely to object were reportedly left off the invite list. The ones who showed up heard about a dangerous “Jacobin plot” to take over Paris. No such plot was ever proven.

Step 2: Move the stage. “For safety,” the lawmakers voted to move both houses out of Paris to the palace of Saint-Cloud, away from crowds. They also put Napoleon in command of every soldier in the city.

Step 3: Empty the government. Sieyès and Ducos resigned. Talleyrand went to see Director Barras, who signed a resignation letter. Stories say Talleyrand brought a bribe of up to 2 million francs, and that he may have kept it. Nobody has proven either. The last two Directors were held under guard at their palace. The guard was General Moreau, the man who had turned down the job.
France went to bed with no government.
The Market Placed Its Bet
Paris had a stock exchange, and it traded French government bonds. Those bond prices tell you what the money men thought of the government.

At the end of September 1799, a 100-franc government bond sold for about 7 francs. Investors thought the government was close to broke. The price climbed as good news came in from the war and Napoleon came home. The day before the coup it stood at 11.38.

Then came the morning of the coup. The exchange opened while troops were moving and nobody knew how it would end. The price jumped to 12.88, “before the result was secure,” as one historian put it. Within a week it hit 20.
In seven weeks the bonds nearly tripled. Somebody was betting on the coup while it was happening.

blocks.text: The price nearly tripled in seven weeks. The jump to 12.88 came “before the result was secure,” as one historian put it. No proof anyone traded on inside knowledge before the coup began. Source: Napoleon – Sources.

The official version, printed in 1800: deputies lunge at Bonaparte in the Orangerie at Saint-Cloud on 19 Brumaire (10 November 1799). The daggers were the coup’s own story. Isidore Stanislas Helman after Charles Monnet. Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam. Public domain.

There’s no proof anyone traded on inside knowledge before the coup began. The famous story of Talleyrand bragging that he bought bonds the day before was first printed about 70 years later. Still, the market voted fast, and it voted yes.
Day Two: The Hired Muscle Nearly Blows It
On November 10 at Saint-Cloud, Napoleon almost wrecked everything.

His speech to the upper house rambled. Then he walked into the lower house uninvited, surrounded by soldiers. Lawmakers shoved him and shouted “Outlaw him!” In France in 1799, being outlawed could mean execution without a trial. Napoleon was pulled out of the room, reportedly shaken.

His brother saved him. Lucien, as president of the house, refused to call the vote. He went outside, told the troops that lawmakers were attacking their general, and pointed a sword at Napoleon’s chest. He swore he would kill his own brother if Napoleon ever betrayed the Republic. The soldiers marched in with bayonets and cleared the hall.
That night, a small group of lawmakers who stayed behind voted to hand power to three “Consuls”: Sieyès, Ducos and Napoleon.
The “great man” of history needed his little brother to rescue him from his own coup.
Follow the Money
Coups cost money. Troops need paying, officials need persuading and a new government needs cash on day one. So who paid?

The motive. In August 1799 the government hit the rich with a “forced loan,” a heavy tax on the wealthiest families. Jean-Frédéric Perregaux, the best-connected banker in Paris, was in the top bracket. The richest people in France had a big reason to want this government gone.
The cash on the table. The money we can trace came first from army suppliers:

items: Jean-Pierre Collot, a rich army supplier, rented the house near Saint-Cloud that Talleyrand used as a backup headquarters. Roederer, one of the plotters, wrote that Collot “put 500 louis in my pockets” during the coup. A memoir published under Fouché’s name claims Collot lent 2 million francs.
Michel jeune, another supplier, later claimed in a letter that he had advanced 2 million francs on the first day of the coup. He wanted to be paid back, so treat it with care.
The police cash box. See “The Cop Who Looked Away.”

blocks.text: The bankers in the room. The big bankers stayed quiet, but they were close.

items: Le Couteulx de Canteleu, a banker, met Napoleon on October 30. The next day he met Sieyès, Talleyrand, Roederer and Boulay. According to his own memoir, on the morning of day two he was offered the job of finance minister. His banking house had helped Josephine buy her country home that spring.
Perregaux bought a country estate on October 31, nine days before the coup. He put it in the name of a young nephew.

Michel Simons, a businessman in Talleyrand’s circle, hosted Talleyrand and three other plotters at his house on the evening of day two. “Dinner was waiting for us,” one of them wrote. Talleyrand had been a witness at Simons’s wedding two years earlier.

blocks.text: The Gold Pipeline
Simons had done big business with the French government before.

On January 14, 1797, he signed a contract to bring 15,000 to 20,000 British gold coins, called guineas, into France every month. France’s finance minister wrote that one goal was “to harm England through the extraction of its hard currency.” In plain English: drain Britain’s gold.

Six weeks later, on February 26, 1797, the Bank of England ran so low on gold that it stopped paying out coins at all. It stayed that way for more than twenty years. Economic historians list France’s hunger for gold as one of the causes. At the promised rate, a year of Simons’s deliveries would have equaled about a fifth of the gold the Bank had left at its lowest point.

The catch: no record shows how many coins Simons actually moved, and the contract names no British seller. Someone in Britain would have had to sell him the gold. We still don’t know who, or whether anyone did.
The Payoff
Within about a week of the coup, the forced loan on the rich was repealed.
Two weeks after the coup, Napoleon called the top bankers to his office. They promised 12 million francs and delivered 3 million.
Perregaux was made a senator on Christmas Day.

Ten weeks after the coup, the government signed the order founding the Banque de France. It was a private bank owned by its shareholders, with special favors from the state. Napoleon’s name was first on the list of shareholders. Perregaux later ran its governing council and sent Napoleon regular reports on it.

The new bank moved fast to swallow its biggest rival. When some of the rival’s owners refused to go along, a top Paris police official named Dubois arrested them. According to a 2019 study drawing on the Banque de France’s own historian, Dubois received 20 free shares of the bank in return. A month later he became Paris’s first prefect of police.

Historian Mark Stokle, who wrote a 2020 study of these bankers, puts it bluntly: “The financial victors of Brumaire were unquestionably the bankers.” He adds that the deal for the Banque “may have been agreed prior to the coup, although it could also have been determined” at Napoleon’s meeting with the bankers two weeks after it.

The army suppliers who fronted the risky cash got a very different ending. None of them got a seat on the Banque’s council. Collot, Stokle writes, “was snubbed by Bonaparte despite advancing large sums.” Ouvrard, another big supplier, had refused to lend Napoleon money and was left out of the plot. He was arrested within three months.
The people who took the risk got burned. The people who waited got a bank.
The Old Club
Rewind to 1790. A political club called the Société de 1789 met in Paris. Its members included:

items: Four of the seven civilian plotters of 1799: Sieyès, Talleyrand, Roederer and Cabanis.
Five future leaders of the Banque de France.
Walter Boyd, a British banker who, three years later, was raising war loans for Britain’s prime minister.

blocks.text: The club had about 400 members, and it was a small, rich world, so shared membership alone proves nothing. It does show that the men who planned the coup and the men who got the bank had known each other for ten years.
So Who Really Pulled the Strings?
Ranked by what the evidence shows:

items: 1. Sieyès and the government insiders. They wrote the plan, picked the general, invented the threat and ran the vote. Proven.
2. Talleyrand. The matchmaker. He connected the general, the plotters and the money men, and he dined with them on the night of the coup. Proven for his role; his profits are Likely.
3. Fouché. The police minister who kept the plot out of his own reports and had a cash box nobody could audit. The silence is documented; the payments are not.

4. The Paris bankers. They had the motive, sat in the meetings and walked away with the prize. What’s missing is proof they paid for the coup before it happened. Motive and payoff proven; payment not proven.
5. The army suppliers. They fronted the cash, then got cut out. Likely, mostly from memoirs.

6. Napoleon. The hired sword. He was the last man added to the plan and nearly got himself outlawed on day two. Some historians argue he took over the plan in the final days and bent it to his own purposes.

blocks.text: And Britain? No record shows British money anywhere near this coup. Britain didn’t bring Napoleon home either, though a British officer’s newspapers did give him the reason to go. But the men around the table had London bank accounts and London friends, and about two months after the coup, one of the British prime minister’s closest advisers suggested using Perregaux as a private line to Napoleon.
The Twist
The insiders thought they had hired a sword they could put back in its case. Within weeks Napoleon pushed Sieyès aside. Within five years he made himself Emperor.
The politicians lost their gamble. The bankers didn’t. Napoleon took the throne. They kept the bank.
What We Can Prove / What We Can’t
Proven:

items: Sieyès planned to overthrow his own government and chose Napoleon after others fell through.
Fouché, Talleyrand and Lucien were inside the plot.
Sidney Smith’s newspapers reached Napoleon weeks before he left Egypt.
Bond prices jumped on the morning of the coup, before anyone knew it would work.
The gold contract was signed six weeks before the Bank of England stopped paying out gold.
The forced loan was repealed right after the coup.
The Banque de France was founded ten weeks later, with Napoleon first on its list of shareholders.

blocks.text: Likely:

items: Collot’s cash at Saint-Cloud (eyewitness memoir).
The offer of the finance ministry to Le Couteulx (his own memoir).
Dubois’s 20 free bank shares (one specialist study; the original document hasn’t been published).

blocks.text: Not proven:

items: That bankers paid for the coup in advance. Stokle writes that “it is conceivable that individual bankers did advance funds,” but he rejects the idea that the banking world as a whole backed Napoleon.
That Fouché’s police money paid for the coup.
That Britain wanted Napoleon to go home.
That anyone sold Simons British gold.
Any British money in the coup.
The Barras bribe, and Talleyrand’s bond trade.

blocks.text: The other side. The Banque de France’s own history archivist, Arnaud Manas, wrote the one study devoted to who paid for the coup. He called it “the myth of the thirty pieces of silver,” the price Judas took to betray Jesus. His verdict: the story that bankers bought Napoleon’s coup is unproven, and it grew out of political slogans from the 1920s and 1930s. Most historians agree the big bankers waited until the coup worked and then collected. Of course, the bank’s own historian has a reason to defend how it was born.

Why the gap? Maybe there was no secret deal, and the bankers simply knew a winner when they saw one. Or maybe deals like this were made in private rooms and paid in gold coin, which leaves no paper trail. Either way, the people who planned the coup and the people who profited from it were sitting at the same table.
Every coup has investors. Here’s how the returns came in.
